title: The Lapérouse Expedition
traveller: Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse
intro: Lapérouse was appointed in 1785 by Louis XVI to lead a scientific expedition around the world with two ships, L'Astrolabe and La Boussole. It was to complete James Cook's Pacific discoveries and correct his maps, and also to establish trade contacts and open new maritime routes.
ending: After leaving Botany Bay on 10 March 1788, neither Lapérouse nor any member of his expedition was seen again by Europeans. Both ships were wrecked on the reefs of Vanikoro, and Peter Dillon found the evidence in 1826.

stops.text: Lapérouse and his 220 men left Brest on 1 August 1785 in L'Astrolabe and La Boussole, and rounded Cape Horn.
stops.quote: Lapérouse and his 220 men left Brest on 1 August 1785, rounded Cape Horn, and investigated the Spanish colonial government in the Captaincy General of Chile.

stops.text: After investigating the Spanish colonial government in Chile, the expedition arrived at Easter Island.
stops.quote: He arrived on 9 April 1786 at Easter Island.

stops.text: Lapérouse sailed to the Hawaiian Islands, where he and his crew became the first Europeans to set foot on Maui. James Cook had charted the island in 1778 and traded with the people from his ships.
stops.quote: He then sailed to the Sandwich Islands, the present-day Hawaiian Islands, where he and his crew became the first Europeans to set foot on the island of Maui.

stops.text: Lapérouse landed near Mount Saint Elias in late June and explored. On 13 July a barge and two longboats carrying 21 men were lost in the heavy currents of the bay he called Port des Français. The men had visited the Tlingit people.
stops.quote: On 13 July 1786 a barge and two longboats, carrying 21 men, were lost in the heavy currents of the bay called Port des Français by Lapérouse, but now known as Lituya Bay.

stops.text: Lapérouse reached the Presidio of Monterey in Spanish Las Californias and examined the Spanish settlements and missions. He wrote critically of the missionaries' treatment of the California indigenous peoples and likened conditions at a mission to a slave plantation.
stops.quote: He arrived in Monterey Bay and at the Presidio of Monterey on 14 September 1786.

stops.text: The expedition crossed the Pacific again in 100 days and arrived at Macau, where Lapérouse sold the furs acquired in Alaska and divided the profits among his men.
stops.quote: Lapérouse again crossed the Pacific Ocean in 100 days, arriving at Macau, where he sold the furs acquired in Alaska, dividing the profits among his men.

stops.text: After a visit to Manila, the expedition set out on 9 April 1787 for the coasts of northeast Asia.
stops.quote: The next year, on 9 April 1787, after a visit to Manila, he set out for the northeast Asian coasts.

stops.text: Lapérouse saw the island of Quelpart, present-day Jeju. Europeans had visited it only once before, when Dutchmen were shipwrecked there in 1635. He then visited the Asian mainland coasts of Korea.
stops.quote: He saw the island of Quelpart, in the Korean Peninsula (present-day Cheju in South Korea), which had been visited by Europeans only once before when a group of Dutchmen shipwrecked there in 1635.

stops.text: On Sakhalin the Ainu people drew Lapérouse a map showing Hokkaidō and the coasts of Tartary. He tried to sail north through the Strait of Tartary and failed, then turned south and sailed east through the strait that now bears his name.
stops.quote: The Ainu people, Oku-Yeso Island residents, drew him a map showing: their second domain of Yezo Island, present day Hokkaidō Island, Japan; and the coasts of Tartary, Russia on mainland Asia.

stops.text: The expedition rested at Petropavlovsk on Kamchatka and enjoyed Russian hospitality. Letters from Paris ordered Lapérouse to investigate the British settlement in New South Wales. Barthélemy de Lesseps left here to carry the logs, charts and letters to France.
stops.quote: Lapérouse then sailed north and reached Petropavlovsk on the Russian Kamchatka peninsula on 7 September 1787.

stops.text: The expedition stopped in the Navigator Islands (Samoa). Just before it left, Samoans attacked a group of his men at Massacre Bay, killing twelve, among them Lamanon and de Langle, commander of L'Astrolabe. Twenty men were wounded.
stops.quote: Lapérouse next stopped in the Navigator Islands (Samoa), on 6 December 1787. Just before he left, the Samoans attacked a group of his men at Massacre Bay, killing twelve, among whom were Lamanon and de Langle, commander of L'Astrolabe.

stops.text: The expedition arrived off Botany Bay and met the British First Fleet under Arthur Phillip, which moved to Port Jackson on 26 January. The French spent six weeks there, built an observatory and a garden, and sent journals and letters to Europe. Father Receveur died on 17 February.
stops.quote: The expedition continued to Australia, arriving off Botany Bay on 24 January 1788.

stops.text: After taking on wood and fresh water, the expedition left for New Caledonia, Santa Cruz, the Solomons, the Louisiades and the coasts of Australia. It was the last recorded landfall: no one from the expedition was seen again by Europeans.
stops.quote: On 10 March, after taking on sufficient wood and fresh water, the French expedition left New South Wales—bound for New Caledonia, Santa Cruz, the Solomons, the Louisiades, and the western and southern coasts of Australia.

stops.text: Entrecasteaux, sent from Brest in 1791 to search for Lapérouse, sighted Santa Cruz and an uncharted island that was Vanikoro. His ships did not approach it and sailed away.
stops.quote: In May 1793, Entrecasteaux sighted Santa Cruz, now part of the Solomon Islands, and another, uncharted, island to the southeast; this island was Vanikoro.

stops.text: The Irish sea captain Peter Dillon bought swords he had reason to believe had belonged to Lapérouse or his officers. The islanders said they came from nearby Vanikoro, where two big ships had broken up years earlier.
stops.quote: In Tikopia (one of the islands of Santa Cruz), he bought some swords that he had reason to believe had belonged to Lapérouse or his officers.

stops.text: Dillon sailed to Vanikoro and found cannonballs, anchors and other remains of ships in the water between coral reefs. A Tikopian named Pu Ratia showed him the direction to sail.
stops.quote: Dillon managed to obtain a ship in Bengal and sailed for Vanikoro, where he found cannonballs, anchors and other evidence of the remains of ships in water between coral reefs.

stops.text: The wreck examined in 1964 was formally identified as La Boussole. Both ships had been wrecked on the reefs, Boussole first. A group of men, probably survivors of Boussole, were massacred by the local inhabitants, according to the islanders.
stops.quote: In May 2005, the shipwreck examined in 1964 was formally identified as that of Boussole.

notes: Macau: the article gives no date; 'again crossed the Pacific in 100 days' and the following 'The next year, on 9 April 1787' imply 1786 to 1787, so date is given as '1786 or 1787'. Maui, Quelpart and Sakhalin have no date in the article; years inferred from the surrounding narrative (1786, 1787). Left out: Easter Island's Chile call (no place), San Francisco and the Mount Shasta report (no firm date, eruption account discredited), Tonga and Norfolk Island (named in passing). The Samoan attack is placed at Tutuila because the article later says de Langle was killed 'during the expedition's visit to Tutuila'. Fate: islanders' account says survivors built a two-masted craft and left westward about nine months later; unknown what happened. Entrecasteaux's Vanikoro sighting is placed first in the second leg although he never landed.
